5.3 Linear Regression

5.3.1 What is Linear Regression?
So far we have compared means between groups using t-tests and ANOVA. But what if we want to understand the relationship between two continuous variables?


Can you remember what a continuous variable is?

A continuous variable is a variable that can take any value within a range, it is measured rather than counted. Examples from our otter dataset include:

Body length (e.g. 115.3 cm)
Body mass (e.g. 9.52 kg)
Fish availability index (e.g. 6.7)
Spraint count (e.g. 12)

This is different from a categorical variable (such as site or sex), which takes a fixed number of distinct values. In linear regression, the dependent variable (y) must be continuous. The independent variable (x) is typically continuous too, though categorical variables can also be used in more advanced models.

In our otter survey, we might ask:

“Does fish availability predict how many spraints an otter leaves?”

This is a question about a relationship between two variables, as fish availability increases, do spraints increase too? Linear regression allows us to answer this.



5.3.2 The Three Steps of Linear Regression
Step 1: Test whether a relationship exists
We plot the data and fit a straight line, then test whether the slope is significantly different from zero.

If fish availability has no effect on spraints, the line would be completely flat (slope = 0), as fish availability increases, spraints do not change.


If fish availability does affect spraints, the line would slope upwards (positive relationship) or downwards (negative relationship).

The two plots below illustrate this using our otter data:





Figure 1. Left: fish availability shows a clear positive relationship with spraint count. Right: body length shows almost no relationship with spraint count.






Click to show explanation of the plots


Fish availability (left): the line slopes clearly upward, suggesting that as fish availability increases, spraint count increases too. The points follow the line closely, suggesting a strong positive relationship.
Body length (right): the line is almost completely flat, and the points are scattered widely with no clear pattern. This suggests no meaningful relationship between body length and spraint count.


Looking at the fish availability plot, what does the slope of the line suggest?

 As fish availability increases, spraint count increases, there is a positive relationship between the two variables. As fish availability increases, spraint count decreases, there is a negative relationship. The line is flat, suggesting fish availability has no effect on spraint count. The relationship between fish availability and spraint count is curved, not linear.

Looking at the body length plot, what does the slope of the line suggest?

 As body length increases, spraint count increases, larger otters mark their territory more. As body length increases, spraint count decreases, larger otters mark their territory less. The line is almost flat, suggesting body length has little or no effect on spraint count. Body length perfectly predicts spraint count.

Comparing the two plots, which variable appears to be a better predictor of spraint count?

 Fish availability, the points follow the line more closely and the slope is steeper, suggesting a stronger relationship with spraint count. Body length, the flat line means there is no noise in the data, making it a more reliable predictor. Both variables predict spraint count equally well. Neither variable predicts spraint count, both lines are flat.

If the slope of the fish availability line was negative instead of positive, what would this mean biologically?

 As fish availability increases, otters leave fewer spraints, perhaps because they do not need to defend territory as strongly when food is plentiful. Fish availability has no effect on spraint count. Otters always leave more spraints when fish are scarce. The regression assumptions have been violated.

We test the slope formally using a t-test, which produces a p-value:

If p < 0.05: the slope is significantly different from zero; we have evidence of a relationship
If p > 0.05: we do not have enough evidence to conclude a relationship exists

In R, we fit the linear model using lm() and then use summary() to view the results:

lm_fish   <- lm(spraints ~ fish_index, data = otter_data)
lm_length <- lm(spraints ~ length_cm,  data = otter_data)


summary(lm_fish)

For fish index, the slope is significantly different from zero (p < 0.001), confirming a positive relationship with spraint count. For body length, the slope is not significantly different from zero (p = 0.207), confirming no meaningful relationship.
Where would you find the p-value for the slope in the summary() output?

 In the Coefficients table, in the row labelled fish_index, under the column Pr(>|t|). In the Coefficients table, in the row labelled (Intercept), under the column Pr(>|t|). In the R-squared value at the bottom of the output. In the F-statistic at the bottom of the output.

If the t value for the slope is 8.45, what does this suggest?

 The slope is 8.45 standard errors away from zero, strong evidence that the slope is significantly different from zero. The p-value is 8.45, so the result is not significant. The slope itself is 8.45, fish availability increases spraints by 8.45 per unit. The R-squared value is 8.45, meaning the model explains 8.45% of the variation.


Step 2: Assess the strength of the relationship
Even if a relationship exists, it might be weak, the data points might be scattered widely around the line. We measure how well the line fits the data using R² (R-squared):

R² is the proportion of variation in spraints that is explained by fish availability.


R² = 1: the line fits the data perfectly
R² = 0.6: fish availability explains 60% of the variation in spraints; other factors explain the remaining 40%
R² = 0: the line explains nothing; fish availability has no predictive power

R² can be found in the summary() output under Multiple R-squared:

summary(lm_fish)$r.squared

[1] 0.6898364

summary(lm_length)$r.squared

[1] 0.02722733


If R² = 0.69 for the relationship between fish index and spraints, and R² = 0.027 for the relationship between body length and spraints, what does this mean?

 Fish availability explains 69% of the variation in spraint counts, making it a strong predictor. Body length explains only 2.7% of the variation, suggesting it is a very poor predictor of spraint count. Both variables explain a similar proportion of the variation in spraint counts, so neither is a better predictor than the other. Body length explains 69% of the variation in spraint counts, while fish availability explains only 2.7%, body length is therefore the stronger predictor. An R-squared of 0.69 means the regression line fits the data perfectly, while 0.027 means the model assumptions have been violated.


Step 3: Describe the relationship
Finally, we describe the relationship using the regression equation:
y = a + bx
For our otter data:
\text{spraints} = a + b \times \text{fish index}
Where:

y = spraints: the dependent variable (what we are trying to predict)
x = fish index: the independent variable (what we think drives spraints)
a = the intercept: the predicted number of spraints when fish index = 0
b = the slope: how much spraints change for each one-unit increase in fish index

We can extract the slope and intercept directly from the model:

coef(lm_fish)

(Intercept)  fish_index 
  0.2482678   1.8130078 


What does a slope of zero mean in a linear regression?

 The regression line passes through the origin. The independent variable has no effect on the dependent variable, as x increases, y does not change. The R-squared value is equal to 1, meaning the line fits the data perfectly. The intercept is equal to zero, meaning the line starts at the origin.

What does the intercept tell us in our otter regression?

 The rate at which spraints increase as fish availability increases. The proportion of variation in spraints explained by fish availability. The predicted number of spraints when fish index is zero, the baseline spraint count when there are no fish available. The p-value for the test of whether the slope is significantly different from zero.

In our otter model, what is the dependent variable?
Fish indexBody lengthSpraintsSiteSeason






Note



Important assumptions of linear regression:

The relationship between the two variables is linear: a straight line is a reasonable description of the data
The residuals (differences between observed and predicted values) are normally distributed
The variance of the residuals is constant across all values of x: this is called homoscedasticity

We will check these assumptions in the next section.

5.4.1 What Should We Analyse?
In our otter dataset we have many variables: site, season, sex, age_class, length_cm, mass_kg, spraints and fish_index. We cannot and should not analyse all possible combinations. Instead, we start with a clear research question.

Note



A good research question has three things:

A clearly defined dependent variable: what you are measuring as an outcome
A clearly defined independent variable: what you think drives that outcome
A biological justification: why would you expect these two variables to be related?



Before you visualise or analyse anything, complete this sentence:

“I want to know whether x affects y, because … .”

For example:

“I want to know whether fish availability predicts spraint count, because otters may mark their territory more actively in areas where food is more plentiful.”

Once you have your research question, you only need to visualise the variables involved, not the entire dataset.
You want to know whether fish availability predicts spraint count. Which variables do you need to visualise?

Which of the following is a well formed research question?

 Does fish availability predict spraint count in otters, because otters may mark their territory more actively in areas where fish are more abundant? Is there anything interesting in the otter dataset? What do all the variables in the otter dataset look like when plotted? Can we find a significant result somewhere in the otter dataset?



Click to show explanation

A well-formed research question should:

Name a specific dependent variable (spraint count)
Name a specific independent variable (fish availability)
Include a biological justification
Be testable, it leads directly to a specific statistical analysis (in this case, a linear regression)

The other options are poorly formed because they are too vague, do not name specific variables, and do not have a clear biological motivation. Fishing for significant results across all variables, sometimes called p-hacking,is considered poor scientific practice.




5.4.2 The Analysis

5.4.2.1 Step 1: Visualise
Before fitting any model, always visualise the relationship using a scatterplot. This helps us:

See whether a linear relationship is a reasonable assumption
Spot any obvious outliers
Get a sense of the strength and direction of the relationship

There appears to be no relationship, the points are scattered randomly with no pattern. There appears to be a negative relationship, as fish availability increases, spraint count decreases. Is a straight line a reasonable description of this relationship?

 Yes, the points follow a roughly linear pattern, suggesting that linear regression is an appropriate model. No, the points follow a clear curve, so non-linear regression is needed. What does the slope (fish_index Estimate) tell us?

 How much spraint count increases for each one-unit increase in fish availability index. The predicted spraint count when fish availability is at its maximum. The proportion of variation in spraint count explained by fish availability. The p-value for the overall model significance.

 The proportion of variation in spraint count that is explained by fish availability. Whether the slope is significantly different from zero. The average distance of the data points from the regression line. The p-value for the F-statistic.

Note



Confidence interval vs prediction interval:

A confidence interval gives the range within which the mean spraint count is likely to lie for otters at a given fish index, this is narrower
A prediction interval gives the range within which an individual otter’s spraint count is likely to lie, this is always wider because individual observations vary around the mean



Why is the prediction interval always wider than the confidence interval?

 Because the prediction interval accounts for both the uncertainty in the mean and the natural variation between individual otters, individual observations are always more variable than means. Because the prediction interval uses a different significance threshold. Because the confidence interval is calculated incorrectly. Because the prediction interval does not use the regression equation.

Is it valid to predict the spraint count for a fish index of 15?

 Yes, the regression equation can be used to predict any value of spraint count. No, a fish index of 15 is outside the range of the observed data. Extrapolating beyond the data range is unreliable as we do not know whether the linear relationship holds outside the observed values. Yes, as long as the R-squared value is high enough. No, because the confidence interval would be too wide to be useful.

6.2 Type I and Type II Errors
These are the two types of errors can occur when we are testing hypotheses, and they are related to the null hypothesis. We were first introduced to the idea of the null hypothesis in Workshop 4. The null hypothesis is a statement that there is  between the variables being tested.

6.2.1 Type I Error

6.2.2 Type II Error

text:
6.3 Transforming Data

6.3.1 Background to transformations
So far in this module, we have practised a range of statistical tests, including t-tests and ANOVAs. Before running these tests, we always check two key assumptions:

Normality: the data within each group should be approximately normally distributed (checked using the Shapiro-Wilk test and Q-Q plots)
Homogeneity of variance: the variance within each group should be approximately equal (checked using Levene’s test)

When both assumptions are met, we can proceed with a parametric test. When they are not met, we have two options:

Use a non-parametric alternative (covered in Workshop 3)
Transform the data to see whether the assumptions can be satisfied on a different scale

This section focuses on the second option; data transformation.






Note



What is a transformation?
A transformation applies a mathematical function to every value in a variable. This changes the scale of the data but not the relationships within it — the same otters that had higher tick counts before transformation will still have relatively high counts after transformation. The goal is to make the distribution more symmetrical and closer to normal.





6.3.2 Common Transformations








Transformation
R code
When to use




Log
log(x) or log10(x)
Right-skewed data, counts, data spanning several orders of magnitude


Square root
sqrt(x)
Count data with moderate right skew


Reciprocal
1/x
Extreme right skew



The most commonly used transformation in biology is the log transformation, which is particularly useful for count data such as tick counts or parasite counts, as seen in Workshop 2 and this workshop.
What is written in the table may seem a bit daunting at first, but the dropdown below explains each transformation in more detail.


Common transformations in more detail

Log Transformation
A log transformation is used when your data are right skewed. As you may remember from the histograms in Workshop 2, right-skewed data have a long tail stretching to the right — most values are clustered at the low end, but a small number of very high values pull the tail outward.
Log transformation works best when the data are:

Right skewed: as described above
Counts or measurements that cannot be negative — log transformation only works on positive values. Examples from our workshops include:

parasite_count from the wood mouse dataset — the number of parasites found on each mouse (discrete)
tick_count from the otter dataset — the number of ticks recorded on each otter (discrete)
fish_index from the otter dataset — a continuous measure of fish availability (continuous)

Spanning a wide range of values — for example, values ranging from 1 to 1,000, where the high values are distorting the distribution


Square Root Transformation
A square root transformation is a milder version of the log transformation. It is useful when the data are moderately right-skewed but the skew is not as extreme.

If the log transformation overcorrects and makes the data left-skewed, try the square root transformation instead.

It works best for:

Count data with moderate skew
Data where zeros are present


Reciprocal Transformation
The reciprocal transformation (1/x) is the strongest of the three and is used only when the data are extremely right skewed — for example, reaction times or waiting times, where a few very large values dominate the distribution.






Warning



The reciprocal transformation reverses the order of the data — a large value becomes a small value and vice versa. This means results must be interpreted carefully. It also cannot be applied when any values are zero.









Warning



Important: log(0) is undefined in mathematics. If your data contain zeros (which count data often does), always use log(x + 1) instead. This shifts all values up by 1 before taking the log, avoiding the problem.





6.3.3 The Workflow
The key principle is to check, transform, then check again:

   Check normality of the original data (Shapiro-Wilk)
   If assumptions are violated, apply a transformation
   Check normality of the transformed data (Shapiro-Wilk)
   If assumptions are now met, proceed with parametric test on transformed data
   If assumptions are still violated, consider a non-parametric test instead


We will first go through examples of how to do this together, you will then be tasked with applying the workflow to a new dataset in the exercise, and writing the code yourselves.

6.3.3.1 Step 1: Check the Original Data
We will use the tick_count variable from the otter dataset, this is the number of ticks recorded on each otter during the survey.

ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = tick_count)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Tick count", y = "Frequency",
       title = "Before: raw tick counts") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)




Figure 1. Distribution of raw tick counts in otters.



# Formally test normality
shapiro.test(otter_data$tick_count)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  otter_data$tick_count
W = 0.83418, p-value = 1.072e-06


What does the histogram tell us about the distribution of tick counts?

 The data are strongly right-skewed, most otters have very few or no ticks, but a small number have very high counts. This suggests a log transformation may be appropriate. The data are approximately normally distributed and no transformation is needed. The data are left-skewed, so a log transformation would not be appropriate. The histogram tells us nothing about whether transformation is needed.




6.3.3.2 Step 2: Apply the Log Transformation

otter_data <- otter_data %>%
  mutate(log_tick_count = log(tick_count + 1))

Note



Why are we using log(x + 1) and not just log(x)?
Some otters in this dataset have a tick count of 0, they had no ticks recorded during the survey. log(0) is undefined and R will return -Inf. Adding 1 to every value before taking the log avoids this problem, while having a very small effect on the shape of the distribution.





6.3.3.3 Step 3: Check the Transformed Data

plot_tick_raw <- ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = tick_count)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Tick count", y = "Frequency",
       title = "Before: raw tick counts") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

plot_tick_log <- ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = log_tick_count)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, fill = "#7CAE00", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Log(tick count + 1)", y = "Frequency",
       title = "After: log-transformed tick counts") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

plot_tick_raw + plot_tick_log




Figure 2. Raw (left) vs log-transformed (right) tick counts. The transformation makes the distribution more symmetrical.



# Check normality of transformed data
shapiro.test(otter_data$log_tick_count)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  otter_data$log_tick_count
W = 0.96763, p-value = 0.1117


Comparing the two histograms, what effect has the log transformation had?

 The transformation has made the distribution more right-skewed by spreading the high values further apart from the low values. The transformation has had no effect on the shape of the distribution, both histograms look identical regardless of the scale used. The transformation has pulled the long right tail back in, making the distribution more symmetrical and closer to normal. The transformation has removed all the zeros from the data, which is why the distribution looks different after transformation.

Why do we use log(tick_count + 1) rather than log(tick_count)?

 Adding 1 makes the transformation more powerful by increasing all values before the log is applied, which improves the shape of the distribution. R cannot calculate log values for integers, so adding 1 converts the counts to decimals that R can process correctly. Some otters have a tick count of 0, and log(0) is undefined, adding 1 ensures all values are positive before the transformation is applied. The tick counts need to be standardised before transformation, and adding 1 shifts all values onto a comparable scale.




6.3.3.4 Step 4: Decide Whether to Proceed
After transformation, we check the Shapiro-Wilk test again:

If p > 0.05: the transformed data are approximately normal; proceed with a parametric test using log_tick_count
If p < 0.05: the transformation has not resolved the issue; consider a non-parametric test instead

In our case, the Shapiro-Wilk test returns p = 0.112 after log transformation, the tick count data are now approximately normally distributed and we can proceed with a parametric test.

# Run a t-test on the log-transformed tick counts by sex
t.test(log_tick_count ~ sex, data = otter_data, var.equal = TRUE)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  log_tick_count by sex
t = 0.14374, df = 58, p-value = 0.8862
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group female and group male is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.3234387  0.3734845
sample estimates:
mean in group female   mean in group male 
            1.325001             1.299978 








Note



Interpreting results on a transformed scale:
When you transform your data, your results are on the transformed scale. For example, the t-test above compares log(tick_count + 1) between male and female otters. The difference between groups is expressed in log units, not raw tick counts. This is worth mentioning when writing up your results.


If the Shapiro-Wilk test still returns p < 0.05 after log transformation, what should you do?

 Keep trying different transformations such as square root or reciprocal until one produces a p-value above 0.05. Use a non-parametric alternative such as the Mann-Whitney U test or Kruskal-Wallis test, which do not require the data to be normally distributed. Proceed with the parametric test anyway, as a single failed Shapiro-Wilk test is not sufficient reason to abandon a parametric approach. Remove any outliers from the dataset and rerun the transformation, as extreme values are likely causing the test to fail.







Warning



Transformation is not always the answer. If the data are still non-normal after transformation, do not keep trying different transformations until one works. Instead, use a non-parametric test. Refer back to the parametric vs non-parametric table in Workshop 3.

6.4 When Transformation Does Not Work
To illustrate that transformation does not always solve the problem, let us revisit the parasite_count variable from the wood mouse dataset in Workshop 2. We found that this variable is also right-skewed, but has a much larger proportion of zeros, as most mice had no parasites at all.
Let’s compare the plots below to compare the raw and transformed parasite count variable.

mice_parasites <- mice_parasites %>%
  mutate(log_parasite_count = log(parasite_count + 1))

plot_mice_raw <- ggplot(mice_parasites, aes(x = parasite_count)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Parasite count", y = "Frequency",
       title = "Before: raw parasite counts") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

plot_mice_log <- ggplot(mice_parasites, aes(x = log_parasite_count)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, fill = "#F8766D", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Log(parasite count + 1)", y = "Frequency",
       title = "After: log-transformed parasite counts") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

plot_mice_raw + plot_mice_log




Figure 3. Raw (left) vs log-transformed (right) parasite counts in wood mice. The large number of zeros means the transformation is less successful.




We can also see this in the Shapiro-Wilk test results below, which show that the parasite count data are significantly non-normal both before and after log transformation (p < 0.05).

shapiro.test(mice_parasites$parasite_count)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  mice_parasites$parasite_count
W = 0.61992, p-value = 3.351e-11

shapiro.test(mice_parasites$log_parasite_count)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  mice_parasites$log_parasite_count
W = 0.79101, p-value = 8.114e-08








Note



Even after log transformation, the parasite count data remain significantly “non-normal” (p < 0.05). This is because the large number of zeros creates a spike at the left end of the distribution that transformation cannot remove. In this case, a non-parametric test would be the appropriate choice.
This contrast between the tick count data (transformation successful) and the parasite count data (transformation unsuccessful) illustrates an important principle: log transformation works best when zeros are relatively rare.


Comparing the tick count and parasite count results, what is the key difference that determines whether log transformation is successful?

 The parasite count data contain a much larger proportion of zeros, which creates a spike that log transformation cannot remove — the tick count data have fewer zeros and transform more successfully. The tick count data have a smaller mean and lower variance than the parasite count data, which makes them easier to normalise regardless of their distribution. The parasite count data come from a different type of survey and were collected using a different method, which affects how well transformations work on the data. Log transformation always works for right-skewed count data — the parasite count transformation must have failed due to a coding error rather than a property of the data itself.

6.5 Non-Parametric Alternatives
When transformation does not work, we can use a non-parametric test instead. Non-parametric tests do not assume that the data are normally distributed, and they make no assumptions about the distribution of the data at all. They do not work by predicting the likely values of population parameters from sample statistics.
If you remember from Workshop 3, we introduced the concept of non-parametric equivalents. The table below serves as a reminder:

Common parametric tests and their non-parametric equivalents (Field, A. (2024))






Parametric test
Non-parametric equivalent




One-sample t-test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test


Two-sample t-test (unpaired)
Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon rank-sum test


Two-sample t-test (paired)
Wilcoxon signed-rank test


Pearson correlation
Spearman correlation


One-way ANOVA
Kruskal-Wallis test


Randomised block two-way ANOVA
Friedman’s test




As discussed in the Main Workbook, non-parametric tests achieve this in one of three ways:

6.5.1 Median Tests
Most parametric tests compare means. For example, a t-test compares the mean of one group to the mean of another, an ANOVA compares the means of multiple groups, and linear regression asks whether the mean of one variable changes in relation to another. However, when the data are skewed, the mean is pulled in the direction of the skew and no longer represents where most of the data sit.
Rather than comparing means, median tests compare medians. Because the median is the middle value, it is far less affected by extreme values and skew. Use the tabs below to switch between the mean and median plots and see the difference:

MedianMean







Figure 4. Median parasite count by sex in wood mice. The line inside each box shows the median — notice how low it is compared to the mean.

  sex   median
  <chr>  <dbl>
1 F          1
2 M          0









Figure 4. Mean parasite count by sex in wood mice. Error bars show one standard deviation. Notice how much higher the mean is compared to the median — it is being pulled upward by a small number of mice with very high parasite counts.






# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sex    mean
  <chr> <dbl>
1 F      4.08
2 M      2.91





Comparing the two tabs, what do you notice about the difference between the mean and median for each group?

 The mean and median are identical for both groups, suggesting the parasite count data are symmetrically distributed around a central value. The median is higher than the mean for both groups, showing that the extreme values are pulling the median upward rather than the mean. The mean is higher than the median for both groups, showing that the extreme values are pulling the mean upward — the median gives a more representative picture of the typical mouse. The mean and median differ only for female mice, suggesting that the distribution of parasite counts is skewed in females but not in males.

Looking at the plot, why is the median a better measure of centre than the mean for this dataset?

 The median is unaffected by the small number of mice with very high parasite counts, making it a more representative summary of where most of the data sit. The mean is calculated incorrectly for count data, the median should always be used when working with whole numbers. The median is always the better measure of centre regardless of the data type, as it is less sensitive to variation in the dataset. The mean and median are similar enough here that either would be an equally valid measure of centre for this dataset.




6.5.2 Rank Tests
Rather than using the actual values, the data are sorted into order and each observation is assigned a rank. The test then examines whether one group tends to rank consistently higher than another. Because the test uses ranks rather than raw values, it is not affected by skew or extreme values, making it a good choice for data that violate the normality assumption.
The table below shows how the ranking process works using parasite counts from a small sample of wood mice:


   host_id sex parasite_count rank

2     H002   M              0 15.5

Rather than asking “is the mean parasite count higher in males or females?”, a rank test asks “do males tend to have higher ranks than females?”

Raw valuesRanked values







Figure 5. Raw parasite counts by sex.











Figure 5. Ranked parasite counts by sex.







Comparing the two tabs, what effect does ranking have on the data?

 Ranking spreads the extreme values further apart, making the distribution more skewed than the raw values. Ranking produces the same distribution as the raw values but rescaled to run from 1 to 60. Ranking replaces each value with its position in order, so extreme values have no more influence on the test than any other observation. Ranking removes the zeros from the data so that the test is not affected by mice with no parasites.

When comparing two groups, we use the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (also called the Mann-Whitney U test), the rank-based equivalent of a two-sample t-test:

wilcox.test(parasite_count ~ sex, data = mice_parasites)


    Wilcoxon rank sum exact test

data:  parasite_count by sex
W = 469.5, p-value = 0.664
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0


When comparing more than two groups, we use the Kruskal-Wallis test. The rank-based equivalent of a one-way ANOVA.

kruskal.test(spraints ~ site, data = otter_data)


    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  spraints by site
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 43.302, df = 2, p-value = 3.955e-10








Note



Understanding the test statistics:

The Wilcoxon rank-sum test (also called the Mann-Whitney U test) produces a W statistic: if large enough relative to a critical value, it indicates a significant difference between the two groups.
The Kruskal-Wallis test produces a chi-squared statistic (sometimes called H). The larger the value, the more evidence that at least one group has a different rank distribution from the others

In both cases, the p-value tells us whether the result is statistically significant (p < 0.05).


What is the key difference between a rank test and a parametric test?

 A rank test replaces the actual values with their rank order, a parametric test uses the actual values and assumes they are normally distributed. A rank test always produces a smaller p-value than a parametric test, as it is more powerful. A rank test can only be used when the data are normally distributed, while a parametric test can be used with any distribution making it more flexible and useable in this scenario. A rank test and a parametric test will always produce identical results, regardless of the data distribution.

If the Kruskal-Wallis test returns a significant result, what does this tell us?

 All possible pairs of groups are significantly different from each other. The test compares every combination and flags those that differ. The data within each group are approximately normally distributed, meaning the parametric assumptions have been met after all. We should switch to a parametric test, as a significant Kruskal-Wallis result indicates the data are suitable for ANOVA. At least one group has a significantly different rank distribution from the others, but a post-hoc test would be needed to identify which specific groups differ.




6.5.3 Patterns of Deviation
Rather than looking at the size of differences, these methods look at the direction of differences. For example, do otters with higher fish availability tend to also have higher spraint counts? We are not asking by how much, just whether the two variables tend to move together.

6.5.3.1 Non-parametric tests for association
When we want to measure the strength of association between two variables, we use a correlation coefficient. The most common parametric version is Pearson’s r, which measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two continuous, normally distributed variables and ranges from -1 to 1.
When the data are not normally distributed, or have been collected as ranks, the non-parametric alternatives are Spearman’s and Kendall’s correlation coefficients. Both are based on ranking data, yield coefficients comparable to Pearson’s r, and a significant result (p < 0.05) indicates a significant association.
To remind ourselves about the parametric Pearson’s r: What does a Pearson’s r value of -0.85 tell us?

 There is a strong negative association between the two variables. As one increases, the other decreases. There is a strong positive association between the two variables, but the relationship is not linear. There is no meaningful association between the two variables, neither is linear. The relationship between the two variables is non-linear, and the correlation coefficient does not capture this relationship.



6.5.3.2 The difficulties of non-parametric tests
Non-parametric tests might seem like an easy solution. If the assumptions are violated or transformation does not work, just switch to a non-parametric test right?! However, there are some important things to be aware of before doing this.
When two or more observations share the same value, they are said to be tied. Most non-parametric tests are based on ranking, and ties create a problem because two observations cannot occupy the same rank position. R handles this automatically by assigning the average rank to tied values, but it is worth knowing this happens.


6.5.3.3 Spearman’s and Kendall’s Correlation
So far in this section we have looked at tests for differences between groups: the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and the Kruskal-Wallis test. But what if we want to test for an association between two variables, just as we used linear regression in Workshop 5.
Both work by examining whether the ranks of the two variables tend to move together, rather than the raw values.
Let’s have a look at a ranked version of the otter dataset, and visualise this with a scatterplot of the ranks of fish availability index against the ranks of spraint count:


   otter_id fish_index spraints rank_fish rank_spraints
1     OT001        6.3       13      25.0          35.0
2     OT002        6.1       14      23.5          42.5
3     OT003        5.1       11       9.5          23.0
4     OT004        7.7       15      43.5          47.5
5     OT005        5.6       13      16.5          35.0
6     OT006        6.0       15      21.0          47.5
7     OT007        6.7       12      31.0          28.0
8     OT008        6.4       13      27.0          35.0
9     OT009        6.8       12      33.5          28.0
10    OT010        7.3       16      38.0          51.5







Figure 6. Ranks of fish availability index plotted against ranks of spraint count.




Looking at the plot, what does the pattern of ranks suggest about the relationship between fish availability and spraint count?

 There is no association. The ranks are scattered randomly with no pattern, suggesting no relationship. There is a negative association. Otters in areas with higher ranked fish availability tend to have lower ranked spraint counts. There is a positive association. Otters with higher ranked fish availability tend to have higher ranked spraint counts. The plot cannot tell us anything about association because the axes show ranks rather than raw values.

Now we have seen how the ranks of the two variables relate to each other, we can formally test this using a non-parametric correlation. Spearman’s correlation is the most commonly used non-parametric correlation in biology. It converts both variables to ranks and tests whether the ranks tend to move together:

cor.test(otter_data$fish_index, otter_data$spraints,
         method = "spearman")

Warning in cor.test.default(otter_data$fish_index, otter_data$spraints, :
cannot compute exact p-value with ties



    Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  otter_data$fish_index and otter_data$spraints
S = 5856.8, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
      rho 
0.8372672 


Kendall’s correlation is an alternative to Spearman’s that handles ties more reliably and can be more accurate with smaller sample sizes. It is calculated slightly differently but interpreted in the same way:



    Kendall's rank correlation tau

data:  otter_data$fish_index and otter_data$spraints
z = 7.2747, p-value = 3.472e-13
alternative hypothesis: true tau is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
      tau 
0.6741445 








Note



Spearman’s (ρ) and Kendall’s (τ) correlation coefficients both range from -1 to 1, just like Pearson’s r, the value has a specific meaning:

1: a perfect positive rank association
0: no association between the ranks
-1: a perfect negative rank association



What is the key difference between Spearman’s and Pearson’s correlation?

 Spearman's converts the raw values to ranks before calculating the correlation, making it appropriate when data are not normally distributed or were collected as ranks. Spearman's always produces a higher correlation coefficient than Pearson's because ranking removes the influence of extreme values from the calculation. Pearson's can be used with any type of data regardless of distribution, while Spearman's can only be used when data have been explicitly collected as ranks. Spearman's and Pearson's always produce identical correlation coefficients because both measure the strength of association between two variables.

When would you choose Kendall’s correlation over Spearman’s?

 When the data are normally distributed, as Kendall's is specifically designed for parametric data unlike Spearman's. When you want a larger correlation coefficient, as Kendall's consistently produces higher values than Spearman's for the same data. There is never a reason to choose one over the other as both tests always produce identical results and conclusions. When the sample size is small, as Kendall's tends to be more accurate than Spearman's when there are fewer observations to rank.


If three mice all have a parasite count of 0 and would occupy ranks 1, 2 and 3, what rank does each receive when ties are handled by averaging?

 Each receives rank 1, as they all share the lowest value. Each receives rank 2. The average of ranks 1, 2 and 3. Each receives rank 3, as there are three of them. The tied observations are removed from the analysis entirely.

text:
6.6 When Should You Use a Non-Parametric Test?






Note



Use a non-parametric test when:

The data are not normally distributed, and does not meet the assumptions of a parametric test
The data cannot be transformed to meet the normality assumption
The data were collected as ranks or represent an index rather than a true measurement
The sample size is very small and you cannot reliably assess normality

Do not use a non-parametric test simply because it is easier or to avoid checking assumptions — always check assumptions first and only switch to a non-parametric test if they cannot be met.

6.7 Case Study: Using it in Action
Now let’s put everything together and see how it works in practice. For this workshop, we will be using a bird survey from a woodland. 60 woodland plots across two habitat types were collected, these were (i) ancient woodland and (ii) plantation woodland, to investigate whether habitat type affects territory count and seed availability.

6.7.1 The effect of habitat on territory count in woodland birds
We loaded up the packages needed at the beginning of this chapter, but we will also need to load the data for this case study. The data are in a CSV file called woodland_bird_survey.csv. Call this data frame bird_data and take a look at the first few rows of the data.






Note



As there are many new functions and terms we are learning throughout this module, there is now a new section in the workbook; a Function Glossary that you can refer to if you are unsure about a function or term. This will be updated throughout the module.



6.7.1.1 Step 1: Check out the data frame
Use some checking and inspecting functions to get a feel for the data frame.


6.7.1.2 Step 2: Check out the distribution of the response variable
The response variable is territory_count, which is a count of the number of bird species recorded in each plot. Use a histogram to visualise the distribution of this variable.






Tip



Task: Write the code to create a histogram of the territory_count variable in the bird_data data frame. Use the ggplot function with appropriate labels for the x-axis and y-axis.











Looking at the histogram of territory count, what can you say about the distribution?

 The data are approximately normally distributed and no transformation is needed. The data are left-skewed, with most plots having high territory counts. The data are bimodal, suggesting two clearly separate groups of plots. The data are strongly right-skewed, most plots have low territory counts but a small number have very high counts.



6.7.1.3 Step 3. Check the normality of the response variable
We have the idea from our response variable that it is right-skewed, but we can also do formal tests to check the normality of the data. Our normality tests are the Shapiro-Wilk test and the Levene’s test.
What assumptions are being tested by the Shapiro-Wilk and Levene’s test?

 Shapiro-Wilk tests whether the means of the groups are significantly different, and Levene's test checks whether the data are normally distributed. Shapiro-Wilk tests whether the data are normally distributed, and Levene's test checks whether the variances are equal. Shapiro-Wilk tests whether the variances across groups are equal, and Levene's test checks whether the data are normally distributed. Shapiro-Wilk tests whether the relationship between variables is linear, and Levene's test checks whether the sample sizes across groups are equal.

W = 0.95157, p-value = 0.01847


Since log transformation has not resolved the normality issue for seed_count, we need to use a non-parametric alternative. As we covered earlier in this workshop, one way non-parametric tests work is through ranking: replacing the actual values with their position in order so that extreme values no longer dominate the analysis. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test uses exactly this approach, making it suitable for data that violate the normality assumption.
Referring back to our equivalents table, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test test is the non-parametric equivalent of a two-sample t-test — which is exactly what we need here, as we are comparing seed counts between two groups (ancient woodland and plantation woodland).












Tip



Task: Run a Wilcoxon rank-sum test to compare seed counts between ancient woodland and plantation woodland using wilcox.test().





    Wilcoxon rank sum exact test

data:  seed_count by habitat
W = 597.5, p-value = 0.02748
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0


Looking at the output, is there a significant difference in seed counts between the two habitat types?

 Yes. p < 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that seed counts differ significantly between ancient and plantation woodland. No. p > 0.05, so we cannot conclude the two habitats differ in seed count. We cannot tell because the data are non-normal. Yes. but the result is unreliable because we used a non-parametric test.

Why did we use a Wilcoxon rank-sum test here rather than a t-test?

 The Wilcoxon rank-sum test is always more powerful than a t-test, so it should be used whenever possible regardless of whether assumptions are met. The two groups had unequal sample sizes, which means parametric tests cannot be used as they require equal numbers of observations in each group. The seed count data remained significantly non-normal after log transformation (p = 0.019), meaning the parametric assumption of normality could not be met and a rank-based alternative was needed. A t-test requires both variables to be continuous, but seed count is a discrete count variable so a non-parametric test must be used instead.







Note



Writing up the result:
When reporting a Wilcoxon rank-sum test, include the W statistic, the p-value, and the direction of the difference. Because the test is based on ranks rather than raw values, report the median rather than the mean:


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  habitat             median_seed_count
  <chr>                           <dbl>
1 ancient_woodland                    5
2 plantation_woodland                 3


“Seed counts were significantly higher in ancient woodland than plantation woodland (Wilcoxon rank-sum: W = 597.5, p = 0.027). Median seed count was 5 in ancient woodland compared to 3 in plantation woodland.”


When writing up the result of a Wilcoxon rank-sum test, which measure of centre should you report?

 The median, because the Wilcoxon rank-sum test is based on ranks and the median is a more appropriate measure of centre for non-normal data. The mean, because it is always the standard measure of centre in biology. Both the mean and the median. Neither, non-parametric tests do not require a measure of centre.

Across both analyses in this case study, we used two different tests. Which statement best summarises the decision-making process?

 We used a t-test for territory count because it is more powerful, and a Wilcoxon test for seed count because it is simpler to interpret. The choice of test was driven by whether the data could be transformed to meet normality, territory count was successfully log-transformed and analysed with a t-test, while seed count could not be normalised and required a Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Both tests were chosen before looking at the data, the t-test for continuous variables and the Wilcoxon test for count variables. The choice of test was arbitrary, both tests would have given the same result regardless of which variable was analysed.

What is the single most important lesson from this case study?

 Always use non-parametric tests to avoid having to check assumptions. Always use parametric tests because they are more powerful than non-parametric alternatives. The choice of statistical test does not affect the biological conclusion. Always check assumptions before choosing a test, and be prepared to adapt your approach.

7.1.1 Loading packages and data

We will work with the newest version of the otter data throughout. Please read in otter_data_2.csv from the data folder and call it otter_data.

title: 7  Workshop 7 - Data Visualisation
text:
7.2 Understanding ggplot2
Throughout this module we have used the ggplot2 package to visualise our data. It is based on the Grammar of Graphics, which means every plot is built in layers, added together with +. You start with a blank canvas and add one instruction at a time.
Every plot is made from five components:

Data: the data frame that contains the variables you want to plot
Aesthetics: the mapping of variables to visual features, such as the x and y axes, colour and size
Geoms: the shape used to draw the data, such as points, bars or boxes
Labels: the titles and axis labels
Theme: the overall look of the plot, such as the background, gridlines and font size


7.2.1 The syntax of ggplot2
Here is a template. Focus on the syntax and the order of the layers. It makes a scatterplot with a trend line, a custom colour scale, one panel per group and a minimal theme.
ggplot(data = my_data, aes(x = var1, y = var2, colour = group)) +
  geom_point() +                           # layer 1: scatter points
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +             # layer 2: linear trend line
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1") +  # customise the colour scale
  facet_wrap(~ group) +                    # one panel per group
  theme_minimal()                          # clean, non data styling
Which line of the template splits the plot into one panel for each group?
geom_smooth(method = ‘lm’)facet_wrap(~ group)scale_colour_brewer(palette = ‘Set1’)theme_minimal()


7.2.2 Building a plot layer by layer
The tabs below build a plot from nothing. Click through them in order and notice what each new line adds.

1. Data2. Axes3. Geom4. Labels5. Theme



ggplot(data = otter_data)








ggplot() on its own only creates an empty canvas. R knows which data frame to use, but not what to draw.



ggplot(data = otter_data, aes(x = fish_index, y = spraints))








aes() is short for aesthetics. It maps variables to the plot, here fish_index to the x axis and spraints to the y axis. The axes now appear, but nothing is drawn yet.



ggplot(data = otter_data, aes(x = fish_index, y = spraints)) +
  geom_point()








geom_point() tells ggplot to draw each otter as a point. The + at the end of the line is what adds a new layer.



ggplot(data = otter_data, aes(x = fish_index, y = spraints)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Fish availability index",
       y = "Spraint count")








labs() replaces the default axis labels, which are just the column names, with something readable.



ggplot(data = otter_data, aes(x = fish_index, y = spraints)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Fish availability index",
       y = "Spraint count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








theme_minimal() removes the grey background, and base_size makes the text larger and easier to read.



Which line of code adds the points to the plot?
ggplot(data = otter_data)aes(x = fish_index, y = spraints)geom_point()labs(x = ‘Fish index’)
What does aes() do?

 It chooses the shape that is drawn, such as points, bars or boxes, for each observation. It changes the appearance of the plot, such as the background, font size and gridlines. It maps variables in the data frame to features of the plot, such as the x axis, y axis or colour. It adds the axis titles and the plot title so that the figure can be read by others.

What happens if you run ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = fish_index, y = spraints)) without adding a geom?

 R draws a scatterplot by default, because both variables are continuous numeric columns. R returns an error, because a plot cannot be created without at least one geom layer. R draws the axes but nothing else, because no instruction has been given for how to display the data. R draws a histogram of fish_index, because the first variable is always plotted on its own.



7.2.3 Your turn






Tip



You will need the actual variable names, so think back to the code you can use to check out the data, or use the Function Glossary to help you.


Fill in the blanks to build a scatterplot of body length against body mass. You can put either variable on either axis.
The data frame is: 
The variable on the x axis is: 
The variable on the y axis is: 
The geom that draws each otter as a point is: 
ggplot(data = ___, aes(x = ___, y = ___)) +
  ___()


Click to show the solution


ggplot(data = otter_data, aes(x = length_cm, y = mass_kg)) +
  geom_point()









A student puts length_cm on both axes. What will the plot show?

 A scatterplot with a weak positive relationship, because body length varies between otters. Every point falls on a perfect diagonal line, because each otter's length is plotted against itself. An error message, because the same variable cannot be used for both the x and y axes. A histogram of body length, because only one variable has been supplied to the plot.







Tip



A common mistake: the + must go at the end of a line, not the start of the next one. If you put it at the start, R thinks the code has finished and throws an error.

title: 7  Workshop 7 - Data Visualisation
text:
7.3 Aesthetics and Geoms

7.3.1 Aesthetics
An aesthetic is a visual feature of the plot. Position on the x and y axes is the most important one, but you can also map variables to colour, size and shape, which lets one plot show more than two variables.



Aesthetic
What it controls




x, y
Position on the axes


colour
The colour of points and lines, or the outline of shapes


fill
The colour inside shapes such as bars and boxes


size
The size of points


shape
The shape of points


alpha
Transparency, from 0 (invisible) to 1 (solid)



There are two different ways to use an aesthetic, and they behave differently:

Mapped inside aes(): the feature changes according to a variable in the data
Set outside aes(): the feature is a fixed value that applies to every observation


Mapped to a variableSet to a fixed value



ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = length_cm, y = mass_kg, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Body length (cm)", y = "Body mass (kg)", colour = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








colour = sex is inside aes(), so each sex gets its own colour and ggplot adds a legend.



ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = length_cm, y = mass_kg)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#F8766D", size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Body length (cm)", y = "Body mass (kg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








colour = "#F8766D" is outside aes(), so every point is the same colour and there is no legend.



A student wants every point in a scatterplot to be red, whatever the data say. Where should colour = "red" go?

 Inside geom_point() but outside aes(), because it is a fixed value and not a variable in the data. Inside aes(), because every colour setting has to be written inside the aes() function. Inside ggplot() as a separate argument, because the data frame must be told which colour to use. Inside labs(), because the colour is part of the labels that describe the plot to readers.



7.3.2 Geoms
A geom is the shape ggplot draws for your data. The data and the aes() mapping stay the same, and the geom decides how they are displayed. Change the geom and the same data becomes a different plot.
Each geom expects certain kinds of variable, so the main skill is matching the geom to your data.

Key ggplot2 geoms. A geom defines the visual mark drawn for the data, and you can layer several geoms with +.








Geom
Draws
Needs
Use for




geom_point()
One point per row
Two numeric variables
Scatterplots


geom_line()
A line joining points in order
An ordered x and a numeric y
Trends, and means across ordered groups


geom_bar()
Bars, with R counting the rows
One categorical variable
Counts per category


geom_col()
Bars, with you giving the heights
One categorical and one numeric variable
Plotting values you have already calculated


geom_histogram()
Bars of binned counts
One numeric variable
The shape of one variable


geom_boxplot()
A box and whiskers
A categorical x and a numeric y
Comparing a variable across groups


geom_smooth()
A fitted line
Two numeric variables
Trends and regression lines




7.3.2.1 The same data with different geoms
The tabs below show seven geoms on the otter data. As you click through, notice what kind of variable each one needs.

PointSmoothHistogramBoxplotBarColLine



ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = fish_index, y = spraints)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#F8766D", size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Fish availability index", y = "Spraint count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








One point per otter. Both axes are numeric, so each point sits where its two values meet.



ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = fish_index, y = spraints)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#F8766D", size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Fish availability index", y = "Spraint count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








geom_smooth() adds a fitted line on top of the points. method = "lm" fits a straight line, the same one lm() fits. The grey band is the confidence interval, and se = FALSE removes it.



ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = spraints)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Spraint count", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Only one variable is needed. R bins the values and counts how many otters fall into each bin, so there is no y in aes().



ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = site, y = spraints, fill = site)) +
  geom_boxplot(colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Site", y = "Spraint count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








A categorical x and a numeric y. Each box summarises one group, so you can compare groups directly.



ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = site)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Site", y = "Number of otters") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








geom_bar() counts the rows in each category for you. It plots how many otters, not how many spraints.



otter_data %>%
  group_by(site) %>%
  summarise(mean_spraints = mean(spraints)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = site, y = mean_spraints)) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Site", y = "Mean spraint count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








geom_col() draws bars at the heights you provide. Here we worked out the mean per site first and then plotted it.



otter_data %>%
  group_by(site, season) %>%
  summarise(mean_spraints = mean(spraints), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = site, y = mean_spraints, colour = season, group = season)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Site", y = "Mean spraint count", colour = "Season") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








geom_line() joins points in order, and group = season tells it which points belong to the same line. This is the interaction plot from earlier workshops. The lines here join group means so that we can compare the two seasons across sites. A line across unordered categories is not a trend, so do not use one to join raw observations.





7.3.2.2 Layering geoms
Geoms are layers, so you can stack several in one plot. The order matters, because later layers are drawn on top of earlier ones.

ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = site, y = spraints)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue", colour = "black", outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, size = 2, colour = "#F8766D") +
  labs(x = "Site", y = "Spraint count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








The boxplot is drawn first and the jittered points sit on top of it. If you swapped the two lines, the box would cover the points.


7.3.2.3 Check your understanding
Which geom would you use to show how many otters were recorded in each age class?
geom_bar()geom_histogram()geom_smooth()geom_boxplot()
What is the difference between geom_bar() and geom_col()?

 geom_bar() counts the rows in each category for you, while geom_col() draws bars at heights you supply. geom_bar() draws horizontal bars, while geom_col() draws vertical bars of the same type of data. geom_bar() needs a numeric x variable, while geom_col() needs a categorical x variable to work. geom_bar() is used for means, while geom_col() is used for counts of the number of rows.

A student writes ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = spraints)) + geom_point(). Why does this give an error?

 geom_point() can only be used with categorical variables, but spraints is a numeric count. geom_point() must always be followed by geom_smooth() or it cannot draw the plot properly. geom_point() cannot be used when the data frame contains more than one grouping variable. geom_point() needs both an x and a y, and only an x has been supplied in aes().

To draw a regression line over a scatterplot, you add  with method = "lm".






Tip



When you are unsure which geom to use, ask two questions. How many variables am I plotting? Are they categorical or numeric? The table at the start of this section answers the rest.

section: 7.4 Choosing How to Visualise Your Data
text:
7.4 Choosing How to Visualise Your Data
So far you have been told which plot to make. In real analysis, nobody does that for you. You have to look at your data and decide.
Two questions get you most of the way there:

How many variables am I plotting?
What type is each variable (categorical, discrete or continuous)?

Here are the variables in the otter dataset:



Variable
Type




site, season, sex, age_class
Categorical


spraints, tick_count
Discrete (counts)


length_cm, mass_kg, fish_index
Continuous



A decision guide for choosing a plot type:








What you have
A good first plot
Main layer




One categorical variable
Bar chart
geom_bar()


One continuous or count variable
Histogram
geom_histogram()


Continuous variable split by a category
Boxplot
geom_boxplot()


Two continuous variables
Scatterplot
geom_point()


Continuous variable split by two categories
Grouped boxplot
geom_boxplot() with fill =


Two continuous variables plus a category
Coloured scatterplot
geom_point() with colour =


One variable, one panel per group
Faceted plot
facet_wrap()



These are starting points, not rules. Often more than one plot is reasonable, and the best choice depends on the question you are asking.

7.4.1 Challenge 1: How many otters were surveyed at each site?
You want to compare how many otters were recorded at each of the three rivers.
Which plot would you choose?
Bar chartHistogramScatterplotBoxplot


Click to show the code and plot

Step 1: Look at what the data are.
site is a categorical variable. Each row in the data frame is one otter, and each otter has one site written next to it. We have no number to plot, only labels. The question is really: how many rows have each label?
Step 2: See what “counting” means.
This code does the counting by hand, so you can see what the plot will show:

otter_data %>%
  count(site)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  site             n
  <chr>        <int>
1 River Bure      20
2 River Wensum    20
3 River Yare      20


Each site now has one number: how many otters were recorded there. A bar chart draws exactly these numbers as bars. Here every site has the same number, which tells you the survey was balanced.
Step 3: Let geom_bar() do the counting.
geom_bar() counts the rows in each category for you, so you only give it an x variable. You do not give it a y.

ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = site)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Site", y = "Number of otters") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Why the other options are wrong:







Option
Why it does not fit




Histogram
Histograms cut a continuous variable into bins. site has no numbers to cut up.


Scatterplot
Needs two variables, and we only have one.


Boxplot
Needs a continuous variable to summarise, and we only have categories.









Note



geom_bar() or geom_col()?
Use geom_bar() when R should count the rows for you, as here. Use geom_col() when you already have the heights, for example after running count(site). Both draw bars, but geom_bar() takes only x and geom_col() needs both x and y.






7.4.2 Challenge 2: What does the distribution of body mass look like?
You want to know whether body mass is symmetrical, skewed, or has more than one peak.
Which plot would you choose?
Bar chartHistogramScatterplotLine plot


Click to show the code and plot

Step 1: Look at what the data are.
mass_kg is one continuous variable. Each otter has a measured weight, and we want to see how those weights are spread out.
Step 2: Build the plot.
A histogram cuts the range of mass_kg into bins and counts how many otters fall into each one. The shape of the bars shows the shape of the distribution.

ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = mass_kg)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (kg)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Why the other options are wrong:







Option
Why it does not fit




Bar chart
Bar charts count the rows in each category. mass_kg has no categories, so every otter would get its own bar and the shape would be lost.


Scatterplot
Needs two variables. We only have one, so there is nothing to put on the other axis.


Line plot
Joins points in a sequence, such as measurements over time. Body mass has no sequence, so a line would have no meaning.









Note



Try changing binwidth. A very small value makes the plot spiky and a very large value hides the shape. It is worth trying a few before you decide what the distribution looks like.






7.4.3 Challenge 3: Do male and female otters differ in body length?
You have one continuous variable (length_cm) and one categorical variable with two levels (sex).
Which plot would you choose?
Histogram of length_cm onlyScatterplot of sex against length_cmBoxplot of length_cm for each sexBar chart of sex


Click to show the code and plot

Step 1: Look at what the data are.
The question compares a continuous variable (length_cm) between groups (sex). So we need a plot that summarises the centre and spread of lengths separately for each sex, side by side.
Step 2: Build the plot.
A boxplot does this. Adding the raw points with geom_jitter() shows how many otters sit behind each box.

ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = sex, y = length_cm, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(colour = "black", alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Sex", y = "Body length (cm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Why the other options are wrong:







Option
Why it does not fit




Histogram of length_cm only
Mixes males and females together, so you cannot see whether the sexes differ. It ignores the question.


Scatterplot of sex against length_cm
Possible, but weak. The points stack in two vertical lines and overlap heavily, and it gives no summary of centre or spread.


Bar chart of sex
Only counts how many males and females there are. It says nothing about body length.









Note



outlier.shape = NA hides the boxplot’s own outlier points, because geom_jitter() already draws every point. Without it, outliers would appear twice.






7.4.4 Challenge 4: Does fish availability relate to spraint count?
You have two numeric variables and you want to see whether they move together.
Which plot would you choose?
Bar chartHistogramScatterplotBoxplot
Now decide something else: which variable goes on the x axis? Think about which variable you believe is driving the other.
The explanatory variable (x) is  and the response variable (y) is .


Click to show the code and plot

Step 1: Look at what the data are.
Both fish_index and spraints are numeric, and every otter has a value for each. The question is about how one changes as the other changes, so we need each otter to appear as one point at the meeting place of its two values.
Step 2: Build the plot.

ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = fish_index, y = spraints)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#F8766D", size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Fish availability index", y = "Spraint count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








By convention, the variable you think is doing the explaining goes on the x axis and the variable you think is responding goes on the y axis.
Why the other options are wrong:







Option
Why it does not fit




Bar chart
Counts rows in categories. Neither variable is a category, and a bar chart cannot show a relationship between two numbers.


Histogram
Shows the distribution of one variable. It cannot show how two variables relate to each other.


Boxplot
Summarises a numeric variable across groups. fish_index is continuous, so there are no groups unless you force the values into bins and lose detail.







7.4.5 Challenge 5: Does the effect of season depend on the site?
You have one count variable (spraints) and two categorical variables (site and season).
What is the best way to show both categorical variables at once?

 Make two separate histograms of spraints, one for each site, and ignore season entirely. Draw a scatterplot of site against season, with each point representing one otter. Put site on the x axis and use fill to show season, so each site has one box per season. Draw a single bar chart of the total spraints, which combines every site and season together.



Click to show the code and plot

Step 1: Look at what the data are.
The question asks whether the effect of one category (season) changes across another (site). So both categories must be visible at once, with spraints as the measured value.
Step 2: Build the plot.
Mapping a second categorical variable to fill splits each box into side by side groups.

ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = site, y = spraints, fill = season)) +
  geom_boxplot(colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Site", y = "Spraint count", fill = "Season") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








If you would rather show the means and see whether the lines cross, an interaction plot is another good choice:

otter_data %>%
  group_by(site, season) %>%
  summarise(mean_spraints = mean(spraints), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = site, y = mean_spraints, colour = season, group = season)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Site", y = "Mean spraint count", colour = "Season") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








The boxplot shows the spread of the data. The interaction plot shows only the means, but makes a possible interaction easier to see. Neither is wrong.
Why the other options are wrong:







Option
Why it does not fit




Two histograms, ignoring season
Throws away season, so you cannot tell whether the seasonal effect differs between sites. That is the whole question.


Scatterplot of site against season
Both variables are categories, so points land on a handful of grid positions and pile on top of each other. spraints is not shown at all.


One bar chart of total spraints
Adds everything together, which hides both the sites and the seasons.







7.4.6 Challenge 6: Does the length and mass relationship differ between the sexes?
You have two continuous variables (length_cm and mass_kg) and a categorical variable (sex).
How could you show all three variables on one plot?

 Draw a scatterplot of one continuous variable against the other, and colour the points by sex. Draw a histogram of both continuous variables, and use a separate bar for each sex. Draw a bar chart of sex, and use the height of each bar to show the mean length. Draw a boxplot of sex on the x axis, and plot both continuous variables on the same y axis.



Click to show the code and plot

Step 1: Look at what the data are.
Two continuous variables relate to each other, so a scatterplot is the starting point. The third variable, sex, is a category, so we add it as a colour rather than as another axis.
Step 2: Build the plot.

ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = length_cm, y = mass_kg, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Body length (cm)", y = "Body mass (kg)", colour = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








If the colours overlap too much, facet_wrap() gives each sex its own panel instead:

ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = length_cm, y = mass_kg)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#F8766D", size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  labs(x = "Body length (cm)", y = "Body mass (kg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Colour keeps everything in one panel, which makes direct comparison easy. Facets avoid overlap, but you have to compare across panels.
Why the other options are wrong:







Option
Why it does not fit




Histogram of both variables
A histogram shows one variable at a time, so it cannot show how length and mass relate to each other.


Bar chart of sex with mean length
Shows only one continuous variable, drops mass_kg, and reduces each sex to a single average.


Boxplot with both variables on one y axis
Length (cm) and mass (kg) are on completely different scales, so they cannot share an axis meaningfully. It also hides the relationship between them.







7.4.7 Challenge 7: Is tick count normally distributed?
tick_count is a count variable and you suspect it is right skewed. You also want to check whether a log transformation would help.
What is the most useful way to show this?

 Draw a boxplot of the raw counts only, because boxplots always show skew more clearly. Draw a scatterplot of tick count against otter ID, so that each otter is shown separately. Draw a bar chart of the total number of ticks, so that the overall burden is easy to see. Draw a histogram of the raw counts next to a histogram of the log transformed counts.



Click to show the code and plot

Step 1: Look at what the data are.
You want to see the shape of one variable, and to compare that shape before and after a transformation. Histograms show shape, and placing two side by side makes the comparison direct.
Step 2: Build the plots.

otter_log <- otter_data %>%
  mutate(log_tick_count = log(tick_count + 1))

plot_raw <- ggplot(otter_log, aes(x = tick_count)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Tick count", y = "Frequency", title = "Raw") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

plot_log <- ggplot(otter_log, aes(x = log_tick_count)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, fill = "#7CAE00", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Log(tick count + 1)", y = "Frequency", title = "Log transformed") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

plot_raw + plot_log








patchwork places two plots side by side with a simple +.
Why the other options are wrong:







Option
Why it does not fit




Boxplot of raw counts only
A boxplot can hint at skew, but it does not show the shape of the distribution as clearly as a histogram, and it has no transformed version to compare with.


Scatterplot of tick count against otter ID
Otter ID is just a label, so its order means nothing. The plot would not show the distribution.


Bar chart of total ticks
Adds all the counts into one number, which hides the distribution completely.







7.4.8 Challenge 8: You decide
This time there are no options. Choose any two variables from the otter dataset and decide how to plot them.
Work through these steps:

Write down the two variables and their types.
Choose a plot using the decision guide.
Build it one layer at a time: ggplot(), then aes(), then a geom, then labs(), then a theme.
Ask yourself whether the plot actually answers a question.

A student plots site against season using geom_point(). Why is this a poor choice?

 Both variables are continuous, so a scatterplot cannot show the full range of values for each otter. Scatterplots can only be drawn when one of the variables has been transformed using a logarithm. Both variables are categorical, so the points can only sit on a few grid positions and many otters would overlap. The geom_point function cannot be used with text variables, so R would return an error message.



Click to show the explanation and some good pairings to try

Why the right answer is right.
site has three values and season has two, so there are only six possible positions on the plot. Every otter at the same site and season lands on exactly the same spot, and you cannot tell whether a spot holds 2 otters or 20.
Why the other options are wrong:







Option
Why it is wrong




Both variables are continuous
This is false. site and season are text categories, not numbers.


Scatterplots need a log transformation
This is false. Scatterplots work on raw numbers, and a transformation is only needed if the data are badly skewed.


geom_point() cannot use text variables
This is false. R will draw the plot without an error, which is exactly why it is a poor choice. It looks like a plot, but it tells you nothing.

  geom_bar(position = "dodge", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Site", y = "Number of otters", fill = "Sex") +
