title: 7  Workshop 7 - Data Visualisation
text:
7.5 Seeing the Whole Distribution
A boxplot is quick and compact, but it squeezes a whole variable into five numbers. Different plots show different parts of the same data. Here we look at body mass (mass_kg) split by sex, and build up from the simplest view to the most detailed.

7.5.1 Reading a boxplot
Before choosing between plots, it helps to know what a boxplot is made of. Every part comes from a summary statistic:

otter_data %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarise(
    minimum = min(mass_kg),
    q1      = quantile(mass_kg, 0.25),
    median  = median(mass_kg),
    q3      = quantile(mass_kg, 0.75),
    maximum = max(mass_kg)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  sex    minimum    q1 median    q3 maximum
  <chr>    <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 female    4.82  5.61   6.22  7.22    9.97
2 male      7.2   9.39   9.84 10.4    12.5 









Part of the boxplot
What it shows




Thick line in the box
The median, the middle value


Bottom and top of the box
The first and third quartiles (q1 and q3), so the box holds the middle 50% of otters


Height of the box
The interquartile range (IQR), q3 minus q1


Whiskers
The furthest values within 1.5 times the IQR of the box


Individual dots
Outliers, values beyond the whiskers



What does the height of the box tell you?

 How spread out the middle half of the otters are, because the box runs from the first to the third quartile. How spread out every otter in the group is, because the box runs from the smallest to the largest value. How many otters were measured in the group, because a taller box means that more otters were included. Where the average value sits, because the box is drawn around the mean of the group.



7.5.2 One variable, five views
The tabs below show the same data in five ways. Click through them and notice what appears and disappears each time.

BoxplotBoxplot and pointsViolinDensityHistogram



ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = sex, y = mass_kg, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Sex", y = "Body mass (kg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Shows the median, the spread of the middle half, and any outliers. It does not show how many otters there are or what shape the data take between the quartiles.



ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = sex, y = mass_kg, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(colour = "black", alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Sex", y = "Body mass (kg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Adds every otter as a point, so you can see the sample size and any gaps or clusters. outlier.shape = NA stops the outliers being drawn twice.



ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = sex, y = mass_kg, fill = sex)) +
  geom_violin(colour = "black", trim = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Sex", y = "Body mass (kg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








The width of the shape shows where the otters are concentrated. A wide part means many otters at that mass, and a narrow part means few.



ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = mass_kg, fill = sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (kg)", y = "Density", fill = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








A smoothed histogram. Drawing both sexes on the same axis makes it easy to see how much the groups overlap.



ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = mass_kg, fill = sex)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, colour = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (kg)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








The most literal view. Each bar is a count of otters, and the plot is split by sex so the two shapes can be compared.



You want to know how many otters of each sex were measured. Which view shows this best?

 Boxplot and points, because every otter is drawn as its own point and the points can be counted. Boxplot, because the height of each box is proportional to the number of otters in that group. Violin, because the total area of each violin is always scaled to the number of otters measured. Density, because the height of each curve at its peak shows how many otters were in the group.

Which view would you choose to see whether the two sexes overlap in body mass?

 Boxplot, because the whiskers show the full range of each group and make the overlap obvious. Bar chart, because the height of each bar shows the average mass of each group of otters. Scatterplot, because each otter is plotted against the order in which it was measured. Density, because both curves share one axis and the region where they overlap is easy to see.



7.5.3 What a plot can hide
A summary of the whole sample can hide structure inside it. Here is body mass for all otters together, ignoring sex:

ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = mass_kg)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (kg)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








This histogram is not a clean bell shape. What is the most likely explanation?

 Two groups with different average masses have been mixed together, so the histogram shows both groups at once. The otters were measured badly, so the values are scattered randomly and no real shape can be found. The binwidth is too small, so any dataset would look uneven and nothing can be said about it. Body mass is always bimodal in wild animals, so this shape is expected for any species.



Click to show the same data split by sex


ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = mass_kg, fill = sex)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, colour = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (kg)", y = "Frequency", fill = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Males and females have different typical masses, so combining them gives a lumpy shape. Neither group is oddly shaped on its own. A single summary of the whole sample would hide this.






Note



This matters for the assumption checks in this module. A Shapiro-Wilk test on the whole variable can fail simply because two groups have been mixed, so it is better to check normality within each group, as we have done throughout.





7.5.4 Putting a summary on top of the raw data
You can also show the mean on a boxplot, to compare it with the median:

ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = sex, y = tick_count, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(colour = "black", alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 4, fill = "white") +
  labs(x = "Sex", y = "Tick count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








The white diamond is the mean and the thick line is the median.
In a right skewed variable such as tick_count, where do you expect the mean to sit compared with the median?

 Below the median, because a large number of zero counts pull the mean towards the bottom. On the median, because the mean and median are always equal for count data of this type. Above the median, because a small number of very high counts pull the mean upwards. Outside the box, because the mean is always further from the centre than the median is.



7.5.5 Choosing between them



If you want to see
Try




A quick summary of centre and spread for several groups
Boxplot


The summary and the sample size
Boxplot with geom_jitter()


The shape of each group
Violin or faceted histogram


How much groups overlap
Density plot


Whether a variable is skewed
Histogram









Tip



No single plot shows everything. When you are exploring new data, make two or three different plots of the same variable before you decide what it looks like.

text:
10.5 Definitions used in this coursebook

10.5.1 Workshop 2

10.5.1.1 Data Types
Quantitative/Numerical data
Data that can be measured and expressed numerically.
Discrete data
Data that can only take specific values, often counted (e.g. number of students in a class).
Continuous data
Data that can take any value within a range, often measured (e.g. height, temperature).
Qualitative/Categorical data
Data that can be divided into categories or groups.
Nominal data
Categorical data with no inherent order (e.g. eye colour, type of fruit).
Ordinal data
Categorical data with a meaningful order (e.g. education level, satisfaction rating).


10.5.1.2 Summary statistics
Mean
The total of all values divided by the number of values.
Median
The middle value when the data is arranged in order.
Mode
The value that occurs most often.
Range
The difference between the largest and smallest values.
Standard deviation
A measure of how spread out the values are around the mean; the square root of the variance.
Variance
A measure of how much values differ from the mean, calculated as the average of the squared differences from the mean.
Skewness
A measure of asymmetry in the distribution of data. A positive skew indicates a longer tail on the right; a negative skew indicates a longer tail on the left.



10.5.2 Workshop 3

10.5.2.1 Sampling and inference
Sampling
Selecting a subset (sample) of individuals or observations from a larger population to estimate characteristics of the whole population, without measuring everything.
Sampling error
The difference between a sample statistic and the true population parameter, arising because a sample may not perfectly represent the population.
Probability
A numerical measure (between 0 and 1) of the likelihood that a specific event will occur.
Standard error of the mean (SEM)
An estimate of how much a sample mean is likely to vary from the true population mean: SD / sqrt(n).
Confidence intervals
A range of values, calculated from sample data, likely to contain the true population parameter at a given confidence level (e.g. 95%).


10.5.2.2 Testing for differences
T-tests
Test whether the difference between two means is larger than sampling error alone would explain.

One-sample t-test: compares a single sample mean to a hypothesised population mean.
Two-sample t-test: compares the means of two independent samples, using the standard error of the difference between means.

Statistical significance
A result is significant when its p-value falls below a chosen threshold (conventionally p < 0.05) — meaning the result is unlikely to be due to sampling error, not that the effect is large or important.
Parametric test
A test that assumes the data follow a normal distribution.
Non-parametric test
A test that makes no assumption about the distribution of the data.
Q-Q plot
A plot comparing the quantiles of the data to the quantiles of a normal distribution; points falling roughly along a straight line indicate normality.
Shapiro-Wilk test
A formal statistical test for normality.
Levene’s test
A test of whether the variances of two or more groups are approximately equal.

text:
8.1 Multiple Linear Regression
So far, our linear models have had one predictor (independent variable) and one dependent variable. In Workshop 5, for example, we used fish availability to predict spraint count. But most outcomes in biology have more than one influence. Spraint count might depend on fish availability, but also on body length, the season or the river.
Multiple linear regression extends the linear model to two or more predictors used together to explain a single dependent variable. The process is very similar to the regression you already know. We fit the model with lm(), read a coefficients table, and check R² and the F-statistic. The main new idea is how to read each slope.
By the end of this section you will be able to:
crumbs: 8  Workshop 8 - Multivariate Linear Models

title: 8  Workshop 8 - Multivariate Linear Models
text:
Write the equation for a model with more than one predictor
fit a multiple regression in R and read the output
explain what it means for a slope to be estimated holding the other predictors constant
explain why a predictor can add very little to a model


8.1.1 Packages and data
Today you will need the package tidyverse. It is a new workspace, so please install it from the console using install.packages() before loading it into your script with library().
We will use the otter data again, so please read in otter_data_v3.csv from the data folder and call it otter_data.

library(tidyverse)

otter_data <- read_csv("data/otter_data_v2.csv")







Note



In Posit Cloud, packages need to be reinstalled each time you start a new session. If you use RStudio Desktop or Positron, you only install them once, but you still load them each session with library().




8.1.2 A quick recap
In a simple linear regression of spraint count on fish index, what does the slope tell us?

 How much the predicted spraint count changes for each one unit increase in fish index. The predicted spraint count for an otter when the fish index is equal to zero. The proportion of the variation in spraint count that is explained by fish index. Whether the relationship between fish index and spraint count is statistically significant.


8.1.2.1 Step 1: The equation you already know
In Workshop 5 we described the relationship between fish index and spraints with a straight line:
\text{spraints} = a + b \times \text{fish index}
Fitting this to the otter data gives:
\text{spraints} = 0.25 + 1.81 \times \text{fish index}

The intercept, 0.25, is the predicted spraint count when fish index is 0.
The slope, 1.81, is how much the predicted spraint count increases for each 1 unit increase in fish index.

Read it as a recipe. Start at 0.25 spraints, then add 1.81 more for every 1 unit of fish index.


8.1.2.2 Step 2: Add a second predictor
Now suppose we also think body length might matter. We do not change the recipe, we just add one more ingredient: another slope multiplied by the new predictor.
\text{spraints} = a + b_1 \times \text{fish index} + b_2 \times \text{body length}
The only changes are that the slope b is now called b_1, and there is a new term for body length with its own slope, b_2. The numbering just tells the slopes apart.
Fitting this to the otter data gives:
\text{spraints} = -1.24 + 1.84 \times \text{fish index} + 0.012 \times \text{body length}


8.1.2.3 Step 3: Use it to make a prediction
For an otter with a fish index of 7 and a body length of 105 cm:
-1.24 + (1.84 \times 7) + (0.012 \times 105) \approx 12.9 \text{ spraints}
What does the 0.012 tell us?

 For every 0.012 cm of body length, the model predicts one extra spraint, whatever the fish index is. Body length explains 1.2% of the variation in spraint count, with fish index held at its average value. For two otters with the same fish index, the longer one is predicted to have 0.012 more spraints for each extra cm of body length. For every extra spraint, an otter's body length is predicted to increase by 0.012 cm, with fish index fixed.



8.1.2.4 Step 4: Add as many predictors as you like
The pattern never changes. Each extra predictor adds one more slope multiplied by that predictor. Written in general, with x_1, x_2 and so on standing for the predictors, it looks like this:


Click to show the general equation

y = a + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + b_3x_3 + \dots
Where y is the dependent variable, a is the intercept, and each b is the slope for the predictor next to it. For our otter model, y is spraints, x_1 is fish index and x_2 is body length, so it is the same equation as in Step 2.







Note



Each slope is the effect of that predictor while holding the other predictors constant. In Step 2, b_1 is the effect of fish index among otters of the same body length.




8.1.2.5 Step 5: Fit the model in R






Tip



Remember, you can use functions such as col_names to see the names of the variables in your data frame.


To add a second predictor, join it to the first with + on the right of the ~. Complete the code below.
The dependent variable is: 
The two predictors are:  and 
lm_multiple <- lm(___ ~ ___ + ___, data = otter_data)
summary(lm_multiple)


Click to show the solution


lm_multiple <- lm(spraints ~ fish_index + length_cm, data = otter_data)
summary(lm_multiple)

8.1.2.6 Step 6: Read the output
The output looks like the simple regression output, with one row for each predictor in the coefficients table.







Part of the output
What it tells us here

The predicted spraint count when both predictors are 0, the starting point of the equation

The proportion of variation explained by both predictors together (0.692)

Tests whether the predictors together explain a significant amount of variation (p < 0.001)



The output looks like the simple regression output, with one row for each predictor in the coefficients table.







Part of the output
What it tells us here




(Intercept)
The predicted spraint count when both predictors are 0, the starting point of the equation


fish_index
1.84 more spraints per unit of fish index, with body length held constant (p < 0.001)


length_cm

Multiple R-squared
The proportion of variation explained by both predictors together (0.692)


F-statistic
Tests whether the predictors together explain a significant amount of variation (p < 0.001)



What do the p-values in the coefficients table tell us?

 Body length is a significant predictor (p = 0.526), but fish index is not (p < 0.001), once body length is in the model. Fish index is a significant predictor (p < 0.001), but body length is not (p = 0.526), once fish index is in the model. Both predictors are significant, because the F-statistic for the whole model has a p-value below 0.05. Neither predictor is significant, because the intercept has a p-value above 0.05 in the coefficients table.



8.1.2.7 Step 7: Why did body length add so little?
Compare the model with fish index on its own to the model with both predictors:



Model
Slope for fish index
R²




Fish index only
1.81
0.690


Fish index and body length
1.84
0.692



The fish index slope hardly changes, and R² barely rises. This is because of how the predictors share out the variance in spraint count:

Each predictor may explain a unique part of the variance, which no other predictor explains.
Predictors may also share some of the variance they explain, because they are related to each other and carry some of the same information.

Here, body length explains almost nothing that fish index does not already explain, so its unique part is tiny. It is also only weakly related to fish index, so there is very little shared variance either.
Adding body length changed R² from 0.690 to 0.692. What does this tell us?

 Body length explains a large share of the variation, but this is hidden because it is shared with fish index. The model has become worse, because any rise in R² of less than 0.05 means the predictor should be removed. Body length must be a poor predictor in general, so it should never be used to model spraint counts. Body length explains very little unique variation in spraint count that fish index does not already explain.







Note



When predictors share a lot of variance
If two predictors are strongly related to each other, much of what each explains is the same information. Their slopes can then change a lot when both are in the model, and become unstable. This is called multicollinearity.








Note



Adjusted R²
R² can only go up when you add a predictor, even a useless one. Adjusted R² corrects for this by penalising each extra predictor. Here it goes down slightly, from 0.684 to 0.681, which also suggests body length is not improving the model. Use adjusted R² when comparing models with different numbers of predictors.




8.1.2.8 Some terms you will meet
Several of these terms are used for the same thing, so here is what each one means.







Term
Meaning




Dependent variable
The outcome we are trying to explain (also called the response variable). In our model, spraint count.


Predictor
A variable used to explain the dependent variable (also called an independent or explanatory variable). Fish index and body length.


Covariate
A predictor included to account for its effect, usually while we focus on a different predictor.


Fixed effect
A predictor whose effect we estimate directly, with its own slope or group difference.


Random effect
A grouping variable whose levels are a sample from a larger set, included to account for non independence, not to estimate each level.



Covariates:
Suppose our question is whether fish availability predicts spraint count, but we know larger otters might leave more spraints. We add body length to the model so that the fish index slope is estimated among otters of the same size. Body length is then a covariate. The model is the same as before, and only the role of the variable has changed.
Fixed effects:
Every predictor in the models we have fitted so far is a fixed effect. Each one gets its own estimate, such as a slope of 1.84 for fish index, and we interpret that estimate directly. Fixed effects can be continuous predictors, like fish index, or categories, like sex or site, where the estimate is the difference between groups.
Random effects:
Sometimes the data contain groups that are not of interest in themselves. If every otter in a survey were measured several times, measurements from the same otter would be similar to each other, so they would not be independent. Rather than estimating a separate effect for each otter, we treat otter_id as a random effect. This accounts for the clustering by estimating how much otters vary overall. Random effects need a different function from lm(), and models that contain both fixed and random effects are called mixed effects models. We do not fit them here, but you will meet them in later work.
In our model, we mainly care whether fish index predicts spraint count, and we add body length only to account for otter size. What is body length?

 A random effect, because it varies from one otter to the next in the survey. A dependent variable, because it is measured on every otter in the data set. A covariate, because it is included to account for its effect while we focus on fish index. An interaction, because it is combined with fish index in the model equation.

Which of these situations would call for a random effect?

 Every otter was surveyed several times, so measurements from the same otter are not independent. A researcher chose two specific habitats because the difference between them is of direct interest. A continuous predictor such as fish index is added to explain differences in spraint counts. A one off survey measured every otter once and compared the body mass of males and females.







Note



The lm() function can only fit fixed effects. This is why the models in this workshop contain no random effects, and why the otter data are not suitable for one: each otter appears in the data only once.

8.2 Case Study: What Drives Spraint Counts?
In Workshop 5 we found that fish availability is a strong predictor of spraint count. But the otters in our data were surveyed across three rivers and in two seasons, and these might also influence spraint counts. They could even be tangled up with fish availability itself, if some rivers simply have more fish.
Our question: does fish availability still predict spraint count after accounting for river and season?
In this model, spraint count is the dependent variable, fish index is the predictor we care about, and river and season are covariates included to account for their effects. All three are fixed effects.

8.2.1 Step 1: Check the data
Can you remember how to check the variable type of our variables? You can use the Function Glossary to remind yourself of this.
You should be able to see if you ran one of the checking functions that site, season and sex are currently characters (<chr>), which means R treats them as plain text. As we did in Workshop 4, we convert them to factors before modelling. A factor is a categorical variable with a fixed set of levels, and the order of those levels decides which one the model uses as the reference.






Tip



Task: Use mutate() to convert site, season and sex to factors in otter_data, then use count() to check how many otters there are in each site and season. Label this as a new object, and call it otter_data_v2


As this one is a bit new; I’ve hidden the code below - but do attempt to do it first!


Reveal the code


otter_data_v2 <- otter_data %>%
  mutate(
    site   = as.factor(site),
    season = as.factor(season),
    sex    = as.factor(sex)
  )

otter_data_v2 %>%
  count(site, season)

8.2.2 Step 2: Visualise the relationships
Remembering what we learnt last week, what plot do you think we could use for this?

 A boxplot, with river on the x axis and fish index on the y axis, so the rivers can be compared side by side. A bar chart of river, so that the height of each bar shows how many otters were surveyed at each river. A scatterplot of river against fish index, so that each otter is drawn as a single point on the plot. A histogram of fish index for all otters together, so that the overall shape of the distribution is shown.



Click to show explanation

Fish index is continuous and river is categorical, so a boxplot compares the centre and spread of fish index across the rivers. This is the same reasoning as Challenge 3 in the visualisation workshop.

What does the plot suggest about fish index and river?

 Fish index is highest at the River Wensum and lowest at the River Yare, so fish index and river are related. Fish index is highest at the River Yare and lowest at the River Wensum, so fish index and river are related. Fish index is about the same at every river, so fish index and river are not related to each other. Fish index varies only within each river, so the rivers themselves cannot differ in fish availability.

Why does this matter for our question?

 Part of the link between fish index and spraints could really be a river effect, so river should be accounted for. Rivers with more fish must have more otters, so the number of otters should be added to the model. The rivers differ in fish index, so the model should be fitted separately for each river on its own. 8.2.9 Step 9: Why is river a fixed effect?
You might wonder whether river should be a random effect, since the otters are grouped within rivers. Here it is better as a fixed effect, for two reasons:

There are only three rivers, which is too few to estimate how much rivers vary in general.
These are the specific rivers we are interested in, so we want to estimate the difference between them directly.

Why do we treat river as a fixed effect and not a random effect in this model?

 There are only three rivers and they are the specific rivers of interest, so we estimate each river's effect directly. Random effects can only be used for numeric variables, and river is a categorical variable in the otter data. Rivers cannot be random effects, because the otters were all sampled in the same year and in the same two seasons. A random effect would need to be fitted with lm(), and the function lm() cannot be used for a categorical variable.
